description: I'm a coding-focused developer working solo on the SPHEREx challenge. I build Python and web tools, and I've built a working viewer and comparison app for SPHEREx sky images using astropy, Streamlit, and Plotly-style visuals. I'm looking for teammates who enjoy data, visualization, or space science to help improve the detection and documentation.
summary:
SPHEREx Sky Viewer is a small web tool for seeing how the sky changes between two weeks of SPHEREx observations. The main page shows two weeks of the same patch of sky, with three ways to compare them: Blink switches between the earlier and later week, a slider fades one into the other, and a Difference view shows the change, with red for brighter in the later week and blue for dimmer. The example uses data from May 8 and June 19, 2025, from the IRSA archive.
A companion comparison tool lets anyone paste any two SPHEREx spectral image links from IRSA, set the sky position, and compare them. The tool downloads a cutout of the same spot from each week and builds the same views. It runs on Streamlit, and the viewer is hosted on Vercel.
I built this solo, using Python with astropy, numpy, scipy, and matplotlib for image processing, and plain HTML and JavaScript for the viewer. Early on, I tested automatic detection of moving objects. A detector with a planted fake object found the fake object, but on real data it flagged many candidates, most likely noise and bad pixels. So the tool does not report detections, and I've labeled the difference view as experimental.
The main thing I learned is how hard it is to separate real sky changes from instrument differences. Stars that differ slightly between weeks appear as red and blue pairs, even when nothing moved. Any future version should align the frames more carefully and use the full images, not small cutouts.
details: SPHEREx Sky Viewer compares two weeks of SPHEREx observations of the same sky patch. The main viewer offers Blink, a fade slider, and a Difference view, with red for brighter in the later week and blue for dimmer. A companion Streamlit tool lets anyone paste any two IRSA spectral image links, set the sky position, and compare them. Data: The example uses two weeks of SPHEREx Quick Release data from the IRSA archive, May 8 and June 19, 2025. Limitations: Automatic detection of moving objects is not reliable yet. A detector found a planted fake object, but on real data it flagged many candidates, most likely noise and bad pixels, so the tool does not report detections. Stars that differ slightly between weeks appear as red and blue pairs even when nothing moved. Cutouts are small, and the comparison depends on IRSA's server; a busy server may return a 503 error.
